title.en: The Tree-wife and the Spitting Trail

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (2024 print) (1924), tale 67 'The Tree-wife' (told by Thomas White, Maroon Town)

summary.en: A childless hunter wishes a pretty Jessamy tree into a wife, clothes her, and lives with her until another man inveigles her away. Fleeing, she spits at every half-mile of the two-mile road; the abandoned husband sings the Maroon Koromanti death-song at each spitting-place, the spits answer him, and the trail of answers leads him to the door where he takes his wife home again.
summary.zh: 無子的獵人許願美麗的素馨樹化為妻子，為其穿衣、成家；後被他人誘拐。逃亡路上，她在兩哩間每半哩吐一口唾沫；被棄的丈夫在每一處唾沫地唱起馬倫人的科羅曼蒂喪歌，唾沫竟一一應聲——循聲而至，他把妻子領回了家。

sensitivity.note: Wonder tale; the Koromanti death-song (Maroon burial song) is quoted in the source as sung at burials — noted here as cultural context, not reproduced verbatim.

passages.text: It was a man who had no wife and was a hunter-man; he hunted in the bush all day. One day he went into the bush and shot, and coming home he saw a pretty tree called Jessamy — 'O me biddy boy, that is a pretty tree!' He said, 'If this tree could turn a wife to me, I would like to be married to her!' And so it was: the tree turned a wife for him. The woman was naked; he left her at the spot, went home, got clothing for her, dressed her up nicely and carried her home to his house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 67 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: He and the woman stayed a long time, until one day he went out to the bush to shoot and slept out; another man came and inveigled his wife and took her away to his house. When the poor man came home from the bush the next day, he could not find his wife. The frightened woman, leaving one house for the next about two miles off, spat all the way until she got to the other man's house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 67, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The man was in a rage that he could not find his wife and did not know what to do. He sang the Koromanti death-song, the song always used by the Maroons at a burial — 'Jesta be-yo, eh, eh, eh, o! Jesta be-yo, a wi' die-o...' — and at every place where the woman spat, the spit answered him. He went and stood at each stopping-place of half a mile until the two miles were passed; and just as the woman heard the voice of the man, she stood at the door-mouth and saw that the man was coming. The man took his wife and carried her right back to the home yard. Jack man dora, choose none!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 67, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Sammy the Comferee Melted on the Iron Rod
title.zh: 康菲里小哥在鐵桿上熔盡

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 68 'Sammy the Comferee' (told by Thomas White, Maroon Town)

summary.en: Sammy's stray arrow lands in Massa Jesus's yard; the wife detains the beautiful boy all day until rain soaks the Master's washing, and scolds her husband that Sammy is prettier than the Maker of him. Massa Jesus heats an iron rod red-hot and orders the boy to climb it; Sammy melts leg by leg, singing his farewell song — 'Ah, me Sammy de Con-fa-ri-a-e-ro, Gi-ra no, ah, in din ro' — and all the pretty men born into the world thereafter get some of his fat; the ugly ones get none.
summary.zh: 小哥的箭誤落耶穌先生院中；其妻扣留美少年整日，直到大雨淋濕晾曬的衣物，還向丈夫抱怨小哥比自己造物者更俊。耶穌先生把鐵桿燒得通紅，命其攀爬；小哥一節節熔化，唱著告別之歌——『啊，我是康菲里小哥，吉拉諾……』——此後世上所有俊美的男子都分得他的一點脂膏；醜陋者分毫不沾。

sensitivity.note: Wonder tale with syncretic Christian frame ('Massa Jesus'); folk-comic use of scripture names, transcribed from named tellers.

passages.text: A woman had one son, a boy very unruly, who had nothing to do but fire bow and arrow all day. One day he fired the arrow and it dropped into Massa Jesus's yard. He went in to pick it up; Massa Jesus was gone out, but the wife was in the yard, and all the clothes were sunning out of doors. She detained the boy in the yard the whole day until the rain came and wet up all Massa Jesus's clothes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 68 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Massa Jesus came in wet, wanting dry clothes and finding none, he asked his wife what she had been doing all day. She answered that as Sammy the Comferee was in the house, that was why the clothes got wet — and when Massa Jesus pressed her, she replied that if he had been as pretty as Sammy the Comferee, she would have done more. 'I know I made Sammy the Comferee,' said Massa Jesus, 'and if Sammy the Comferee is prettier than me, I will see about it.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 68, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Massa Jesus put up an iron rod, hot as fire, hot until it was red, and sent for Sammy the Comferee. He ordered the boy to climb the iron rod, and Sammy commenced to melt away, singing — 'Ah, me Sammy de Con-fa-ri-a-e-ro, Gi-ra no, ah, in din ro!' — he melted off to his leg, sang again, melted to his middle, to his hand, to his neck, and sang again until he melted off to nothing. When you look at the iron rod, a whole heap of fat is heaped up about it: all the pretty men that come into the world get some of Sammy the Comferee's fat, but the ugly ones don't get none of it. Jack man dory, me story done!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 68, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Grandy Beard-o and the Bull Who Didn't Care
title.zh: 大奶奶碧兒多與無畏的公牛

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 69a 'Grandy-Do-an'-Do' (told by Moses Hendricks, Mandeville)

summary.en: The rich witch Grandy Beard-o feeds no one who cannot name her. A hungry captive girl is sent for water past each separated pasture; cow, mule and horse fear to speak, but the mighty bull bawls the name aloud. Fed and freed, the girl inherits the estate when the old lady, tracking the telltale pasture by pasture, is tossed leg by leg, arm by arm, and finally by the neck into the air — which is why the land goes from hand to hand in legacy up to today.
summary.zh: 富有的女巫大奶奶碧兒多只餵能道出她名字的人。被扣的飢餓女孩穿過一座座隔離牧場去取水；牛、騾、馬皆不敢言，唯公牛大聲吼出其名。女孩吃飽獲釋；老太婆逐場追問洩密者，卻被公牛一次次拋向空中——先斷雙腿，再斷雙臂，最後斷頸——所以至今田產仍一代代易手相傳。

sensitivity.note: Wonder tale (hidden-name witch type, ATU 500-linked). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: There was an old woman, a witch, very wealthy, who lived quite to herself — plenty of stock, horses, cows, sheep, mules, each kind kept in a separate pasture. The old lady's name was Grandy Beard-o, but nobody knew that name. She wanted someone to sup with her, took home a little girl, prepared a meal — and said, 'Unless you tell me my name, I will not give you anything to eat.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 69a (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: She sent the girl out to fetch water through all the pastures, and the girl went along crying, being hungry. In the cow-pasture the cow asked what was the matter, and heard it — the old lady would give nothing to eat unless the girl could tell her name — but Cow was afraid to tell her. The mule wouldn't tell her; the horse wouldn't tell her. In the bull pasture, Bull said, 'Cho! when you go home, tell her her name, Grandy Beard-o' — Bull was a mighty man; he didn't care!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 69a, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The girl hastened home glad to get food at last: 'Your name is Grandy Beard-o, ma'am.' The old lady, indignant, gave her a good feed, then started to find who told her — cow, horse: 'A ring ding ding, mamma, ring ding ding; no me tell.' In the bull pasture Bull confessed — 'Damme, me tell 'm!' She gripped the bull and tossed him in the air; he dropped unhurt. The bull tossed her now; she dropped, one leg broken. Toss for toss, her legs, then her arms broke, until the last toss the bull made — her neck broke. That was the end of her. The girl became mistress of all she possessed, and that is why the land goes from hand to hand in legacy up to today.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 69a, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Grandy Do-an'-Do and the Singing Crab
title.zh: 大奶奶杜安杜與唱歌的螃蟹

region.zh: 牙買加聖克魯斯山莫爾文

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 69b (told by Julia Gentle, Malvern, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: A very bad woman sends her only daughter for river water with a name-riddle death-threat. The forgetful girl is returned empty twice; the second time the Crab tells her to sing the answer all the way home — 'Your name is Grandy-do-an-do' — and the maddened witch travels the pastures interrogating Cow, Sheep, Horse, Duck and Crab, machete in hand. The Crab owns the truth, sinks into his hole, and stays in the hole till now.
summary.zh: 惡婆遣獨女取水，以名字之謎相威脅。健忘的女孩兩度空手而回；第二次螃蟹教她一路唱回家——『你叫大奶奶杜安杜』。惡婆大怒，持彎刀遍訪牛、羊、馬、鴨、蟹追問洩密者；螃蟹認下實情，沉入洞中，至今仍在洞裡。

sensitivity.note: Wonder tale, paired variant of the hidden-name cycle. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: A very bad woman had only one daughter, and said, 'Go to the river for water, and when you come back, if you cannot tell my name, I will destroy you.' Going for water she saw Crab, who asked where she was going: 'Grandy sent me to the river for water and said when I come back, if I cannot tell his name, she will kill me.' The Crab told her, 'When you go, tell her that her name is Grandy Do-an-do.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 69b (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: When she came back she had forgotten the name, and the old woman dashed away the water and sent her back. Going again, the Crab said, 'Sing it all the way!' So the girl went back singing, 'You name Grandy-do-an-do! You name Grandy-do-an-do!' The woman, mad when she heard it, traveled and met Cow — 'You Cow, did you tell the girl my name Grandy Do-an-do?' — 'No, no, me tell him so, you name Grandy Do-an-do!' Sheep said the same; Horse said the same; Duck said the same.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 69b, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: She met Crab: 'You Crab, did you tell the girl my name Grandy Do-an-do?' — and Crab said, 'Yes, it is me who told him your name is Grandy Do-an-do!' She took the machete and chopped after the Crab, and Crab sank into the hole and stayed in the hole till now.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 69b, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Jack and Harry: Four Kind Strangers and the Boy Who Ruins Them
title.zh: 傑克與哈利：四位恩人與敗事的孩子

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (2024 print) (1924), tale 70 'Jack and Harry' (told by William Forbes, Dry River)

summary.en: In the cool morning the brothers beg coffee from an old man in the watch-house — Jack drinks the host's own cup and both flee. Hen, poor lady, and carencro each shelter them in turn; at each rescue Jack ruins it — popping the hen's wing, choking the lady, popping the carencro's wing — until the brothers knock themselves senseless, meet a land turtle, and Jack cuts off the head that Harry had called out of its shell.
summary.zh: 清早兄弟倆向守屋老人討咖啡——傑克卻把主人那杯也喝了，二人被追而逃。母雞、老婦、兀鷹先後施救；每次傑克都親手毀局——彈雞翅、掐老婦、彈鷹翅——直到二人摔得昏迷。醒來遇陸龜；哈利剛喚出其頭，傑克一刀斫下。

sensitivity.note: Folk tale (ungrateful-brother type). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Jack and Harry were going out for a walk. The morning was cool, and they came to an old man in a watch-house. Harry said, 'Old Massa, beg you a little coffee if you have any.' He said, 'Yes, me pickney!' and gave Jack a cup of coffee and Harry a cup. The old man had not drunk his own coffee yet when Jack said, 'Harry, I gwine drink the old man's coffee.' Harry said no; Jack took the old man's coffee and drank it, and the old man took his stick after them and they ran.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 70 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Running, they saw a hen with some chickens. 'Do, me good hen, cover me with your wing!' — and she covered them like her own chicks; the old man came after, saw nothing, turned back. 'I gwine pop the hen wing,' said Jack, and popped it — the hen fluttered after them. They ran to a poor lady standing in the way, who covered them with her coat; Jack said, 'I gwine choke the old lady' — and as he choked her, she shook them out and ran after them. Then a carencro (crow) took them both up on its wing, flying right up into the sky — 'I gwine pop the carencro wing, mek him drop' — and as they dropped, they knocked themselves out of their senses.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 70, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: When they came to themselves, a land turtle was coming. Harry called to it kindly, and as it shoved out its head, Jack cut off the head with his knife — so the two boys, who had spoiled every kindness shown them on the road, ended the day by taking the one quiet stranger that offered no shelter and asking nothing back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 70, ending (1924); not verbatim.

region.en: Maroon Town and Santa Cruz Mountains, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加馬倫鎮與聖克魯斯山

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 71 'Pea-fowl as Messenger' (a, Matilda Hall; b, Oliver D. Witter)

summary.en: Summoned to a lying-in, the midwife auditions the household for a messenger able to sing a man's name — cock, dog and puss fail; the pea-fowl, paid a quart of corn, flies miles singing 'You John Studee, for me master!' until the gambler hears his name from a house-top and rides home, hanging his gold chain on the bird's neck — which is why the peacock wears golden feathers there. In the paired tale the same errand ends in pecked baldness for Bra Peacock and a lump of gold for a head.
summary.zh: 產婦臨盆喚夫，接生婆逐一試鳥——雞、狗、貓皆不能名；孔雀受賄一夸脫玉米，飛行數哩高唱『約翰·斯圖迪，我主人在哪！』賭徒聞名歸家，把金鏈掛上鳥頸——孔雀頸上金羽由此而來。另一版本：同一差事卻以孔雀被啄禿頭、頭頂金塊收場。

sensitivity.note: Etiological bird tales. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: The husband and wife were married people, and the husband a great gambler, never at home with the wife — until the wife was going to have a baby, and the ninth month came. They sent for the midwife; when she came there was no husband in. She wanted someone to go call the husband, John Studee. She called for the fowl, a cock: 'What will you say to call the husband?' The cock crew 'Ko ku ru ku-u-u!' — 'You won't do.' The dog said 'Hoo-oh!' — 'No, won't do.' Puss said 'Me-oo!' — 'Won't do.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 71a (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then she called for the pea-fowl and provided a quart of corn, asking what he would say. Pea-fowl sang, 'You John Studee, you John Studee, fe me master John Studee! There's a pretty gal from Silo, there's a handsome gal from Silo, want the care of a new John bwoy — it almost deh!' — 'Yes, you'll do!' When the pea-fowl flew miles off and did not see the master, he took up the quart of corn and flew away; then he pitched on a house-top and sang his song again. The people said John Studee had been there but had just gone away — that great gambler! He flew another mile off and sang from another great house-top, and John Studee came: 'Who calls my name?' He took up the fowl, got the buggy in haste, took the gold chain from his neck and put it on the pea-fowl — the pea-fowl has the golden feathers round his neck on account of that chain. When the feather came home, the baby was born and named John Studee after him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 71a, ending (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the paired version, Miss Nancy's husband Contavio locked her up when he went to market. Hungry, she begged Sheep, then Billy-goat, to call him for a lump of gold — 'No, my dear, that will not do.' Then Bra Peacock flew right away until he saw Contavio, pecked him in his head and picked off all the feathers, and spurred him the whole way home until all Bra Peacock's spurs dropped off. When he got Contavio home, Miss Nancy flung the lump of gold on Bra Peacock's head — that is why the feathers on a peacock's head look like gold, why it has no spurs, and why a crow has no feathers on its head.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 71b 'Contavio' (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: The Barking Puppy and the Phinney Man

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (2024 print) (1924), tale 72 'The Barking Puppy' (told by Alfred Williams, Maroon Town)

summary.en: An old lady's nightly visitor is driven off by the barking puppy; she burns the dog in a big fire — and the ashes bark. Thrown into the river, they bark in the river; thrown into the sea, they hush. At last the gentleman comes in, draws a chair — 'So long I couldn't come on account of Dick and Dandy!' — says he is coming to marry her, sings back her own Phinney-man song, and tears her up to inch pieces: 'sometime shadow come back.'
summary.zh: 老婦的夜訪者屢被吠叫的小狗嚇退；她把狗燒了——灰燼卻仍吠。投入河中，河裡也吠；投入海中，方才安靜。紳士終於登門，拉椅而坐：『這麼久來不了，都是因為迪克和丹迪！』自稱要娶她，還回唱她的菲尼人之歌——隨後把她撕成碎片：影子，有時是會回來的。

sensitivity.note: Duppy-romance tale with violent ending, told as wake-night entertainment. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: There was an old lady living at home with one little puppy, and every night a gentleman came to pay her a visit; but the little puppy snapped and barked, and he had to turn back. The old lady caught the puppy and made up a big fire and burned the puppy. Next night the gentleman came back again, and the old lady sang her song — 'Heah, heah, Phinney man, heah, oh, heah, Phinney man; nobody heah, Phinney man, Dick and Dandy heah!' — and the ashes barked as the puppy. The old lady got up, took up the ashes and dashed them in the river, saying the gentleman was going to pay her a visit and could not, because the ashes barked.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 72 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Next night the gentleman came back again and hollered 'Hulloo!'; the old lady sang, and the puppy ashes barked in the river — and the gentleman would not come. The old lady took the river water and dashed it in the sea to hinder Dick and Dandy from barking. Next night the gentleman came back for the last time; the old lady raised up and sang her song while the gentleman danced, came in now, drew a chair and said, 'So long I couldn't come on account of Dick and Dandy!' — and said, 'I coming to marry you.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 72, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The old lady said yes, but did not know but a dog shadow had come — sometime a shadow comes back. She sang her song again, and the gentleman caught the old lady and tore her up to inch pieces.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 72, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: The Singing Bird and the Well

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (2024 print) (1924), tale 73 'The Singing Bird' (a, Alfred Williams, Maroon Town)

summary.en: The waiting-boy Collin pitches his master into a well at the water-stop and drives home alone with the buggy, reporting visits and delays. A little bird in the tree by the house sings the crime to the mistress — 'Fine waiting boy, fine waiting boy, throw his master into a well' — a sensible person is called to interpret the whistling, the well is searched, the body found, and Collin is hanged.
summary.zh: 車伕科林在取水處把主人推入井中，獨自驅車回家，謊稱主人訪友未歸。屋前樹上的小鳥把罪行唱給女主人聽——『好車伕，好車伕，把主人拋進井裡』——請來通鳥語者解其哨音，井中尋得屍身，科林被處絞刑。

sensitivity.note: Murder-revelation ballad-tale (singing bone type, ATU 780). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: A gentleman had his servant, and one day he said to the servant, 'Collin, go and look about the horse harness, my buggy.' Collin harnessed the master's horse and put it in the buggy; the master drove on till he got to a well and said he wanted some water. 'Massa, there is a well down before.' While the massa sat against the well-side, Collin pitched his master into the well, turned back, and went halfway home with the buggy; when he got home the missus asked where the master was, and Collin said he was going to pay a visit and coming tomorrow — the buggy going to meet him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 73a (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Collin went the next day with the buggy; back at the house again, the missus asked once more where the master was — 'Gone to pay a visit, won't be back till tomorrow.' When Collin was gone, another servant in the yard said, 'Missus, hear what the little bird is singing?' The missus came to the doorway and listened, and heard the little bird whistling: 'Fine waiting boy, fine waiting boy — throw his master into a well! Collin, Collin, no ben see dat little bird upon tree so long?' She could not understand it, called a sensible person to interpret the bird, went and searched the well, found the master's body — and took Collin and hanged him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 73a, ending (1924); not verbatim.

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 74 'Two Sisters' (told by Margaret Morris, Maroon Town)

summary.en: Servant Miss Grace marries her mistress-sister's Busha and bears his baby; the jealous Miss Wheel lures her to pick peas by the sea-ball and shoves her in, taking the baby as her own. Nights on, the dead woman returns to the lying Busha's doorstep, and only the little dog answers her litany — hand me my baby, my bowl, my comb, my clo'es — until the neighbors' pail-of-milk-and-hot-water trap revives her in the sheet, her testimony is heard, and Miss Wheel goes down the hill-side in a barrel bound for the lime-kiln fire.
summary.zh: 女僕葛蕾絲嫁給姐姐侍奉的監工，生下一子；善妒的惠爾小姐誘她到海蝕洞邊摘豌豆，把她推入水中，抱走嬰兒據為己有。此後夜夜，亡魂回到昏睡的丈夫門前，只有小狗應她的連禱——把我的孩子、我的碗、我的梳子、我的衣裳拿來——直到鄰居以奶桶與滾水之計在白布下還魂；她道出真相，惠爾小姐被裝桶滾下坡，送入石灰窯的火中。

sensitivity.note: Murdered-sister revenant tale (ATU 780-linked 'Two Sisters' type). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Two sisters stayed in a house. One sister was servant to a Busha (overseer) in one pen, and arranged for the Busha to marry the other sister — Miss Grace, my fair lady; the older sister, Lady Wheel, served her sister. The Busha went to his work and never came back till midnight. One day when he was out, Miss Wheel called Miss Grace to go pick peas; taking a basket and the baby — Miss Grace my fair lady's baby — they picked peas around the sea-ball, where Miss Wheel made Miss Grace take off her dress and shoved her into the hole. She picked up the peas, came home, washed her breast with water, took the baby for herself, and when night came, suckled it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 74 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Busha came home midnight and was given dinner, but never noticed his wife at all; three days he kept coming and never noticed. When he asked for the servant he was told she was sent out to the common and would soon come. Warned by a neighbor that harm had been done in his house — told not even to drink cold water in the house that night — the Busha lay down at midnight seeming to doze, but not asleep. There was a little dog called Doggie, and Dog saw when the dead woman came.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 74, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The gentleman heard every word; the lady said it was nothing, not wanting the Busha to hear. The last night, the neighbors put up a pail of milk and a pail of hot water at the doorway covered with a sheet; the dead woman came and called out the same litany, took the baby and put it to bed, stepped in the hot water, pitched into the milk covered with the white sheet, was taken out and wrapped up — and she looked up with her eyes fixed. 'What do you, me dear?' — 'My sister shoved me down in the ball. She called me to go pick peas and shoved me in there.' When the gentleman found out his wife had been dead, he took Miss Wheel, built a lime-kiln, shipped her into a barrel, pitched it down the hill-side and rolled it into the fire. Jack man dora!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 74, ending (1924); not verbatim.

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 75 'Asoonah' (told by Philipp Brown, Mandeville)

summary.en: Asoonah, a big-skinned thing that sinks a whole yard, invades the house daily in the mother's absence, interrogating the children — where is your mother, where the pretty little one, where the house with the guinea corn, where's the mortar — until the father guns it down in the gully. The king offers three hundred pounds to name the monstrous skin brought to his gate; the little boy lifts it — 'Eh! no Asoonah 'kin?' — and everybody, frightened, comes right out, and the boy works again with plenty of clothes.
summary.zh: 大皮怪阿蘇那能陷沒整座院落，趁母親外出日日光臨，盤問孩子們——你母親何在、漂亮的小的何在、有玉米的房子何在、石臼何在——直到父親在溝壑中一槍擊斃。國王懸賞三百鎊辨認那張拖到王門前的巨皮；小男孩一舉——『咦！這不就是阿蘇那的皮？』——眾人嚇得四散，男孩得賞，穿新衣重操舊業。

sensitivity.note: Monster-slayer tale. 'Asoonah' is an unidentified large animal in Beckwith's cycle (cf. tale 75 note). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Asoonah is a big-skin thing; when it comes into your yard it will sink the whole place. One day the lady left her three children out and went to work; this Asoonah came in every day, and the children knew what time it was coming — and it asked the small one, 'Where is your mother?' — 'Gone a washing-day.' — 'Where is the pretty little one?' — 'Inside the room.' — 'Where the house with the guinea corn?' and it hollered, 'Where is the mortar?' — 'Inside the kitchen.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 75 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day when the mother came, the children said, 'Every day a big thing comes in here and can't tell what is what.' The mother said to the husband, 'You better stop and see what comes here in the daytime.' He got the gun and went up into the kitchen loft and sat; when he saw Asoonah come, it was so big he got frightened and dodged behind the door, but as it reached the gully he fired the gun and Asoonah fell down in the gully and broke its neck.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 75, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The king heard about this Asoonah but couldn't tell what it was; he said anybody who could come in and tell what it was would get three hundred pounds. The little boy heard about it and was so torn up about it. The old lady keeping a jooty at the king's gate said, 'What way is Asoonah 'kin going to be brought in here today?' When the king asked everybody and nobody could tell, he called up the little boy; the boy went to take it up, and the king asked him if he knew what it was. He held it up like this and said, 'Eh! no Asoonah 'kin?' Everybody got frightened and came right out, and the king offered the boy three hundred pounds, gave him plenty of clothes, and got the boy to work again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 75, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: The Greedy Child at the Devil's Ford

region.zh: 牙買加曼德維爾與馬倫鎮

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (2024 print) (1924), tale 76 'The Greedy Child' (a, George Barrett; b, Philipp Brown)

summary.en: The old ferryman takes breakfast from every child he carries but one — and drowns the refuser, singing up and down the rising water until the mother pays two pounds. In the paired Devil tale, the safe pass-phrase is 'no one go s'y, no two go s'y, no three go s'y, but it go s'y for him mamma' — and the greedy little sister, stuffing herself with the ferryman's plantain, repeats it wrong, is caught over the hill, carried to the river and killed; from that day the Devil's hair came off at the sea-side, and the sea got moss.
summary.zh: 老渡工向每個渡河的孩子討早飯，唯獨一個不給——他便淹死她，任水位隨歌聲一寸寸上漲，直到母親付兩鎊。魔鬼篇：通關口訣是『沒有一個過路、沒有兩個過路、沒有三個過路，只有他為媽媽過路』——貪嘴的小妹吃了渡口的芭蕉，把口訣念岔，被捉過山、拖到河邊殺害；從那天起，魔鬼在海邊掉了頭髮，海裡便生了苔。

sensitivity.note: Paired cautionary tales (river-toll and password types). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: The children were going to school, and every day the old man took them over the river. The old man asked some of them for breakfast; all the children gave him some but one. He appointed a day to come, and said he wanted something from her, and she would not give it. When she was coming back, the river came down; he took over the rest of the children and would not take over that one. The little boy sang, 'Mudder Galamo, I gwine dead today!' — and every time he sang, the water came up a little higher, while the mother was coming. The old man said, 'I must have two pounds'; she said all right, and took him over — and from that day he offered the old man breakfast every day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 76a 'Crossing the River' (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Every night the Debbil went out; coming in he said, 'Wife, I scent fresh blood!' — 'No, me husband, no fresh blood here!' It was the wife's sisters who came looking for her. Every night when the Debbil was coming in, the wife knew and put the sister into a barrel. At daylight he went back over the river; the sister was given a plantain and told that when she reached the hill she would see the Debbil sitting right over it, and he would say, 'Go s'y (go your way), madame?' — and she must say, 'No one go s'y, no two go s'y, no three go s'y, but it go s'y for him mamma,' and the Debbil would let her pass.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 76b 'The Plantain' (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: There was a little small sister, and she was greedy. When the Debbil came in the night he smelled fresh blood; the wife denied it. At daylight the sister sent the little girl away and gave her a plantain; on the hill the Debbil said, 'Go s'y?' — and the little girl, so greedy now, said, 'No, go s'y for mamma, no one go s'y...' — and the Debbil caught her over the hill, carried her right over to the river and killed her. And from that day the Debbil's hair came off at the sea-side; and from that, the sea got moss.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 76b, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Alimoty and Aliminty: the Swapped Frocks
title.zh: 阿莉莫蒂與阿莉明蒂：調換的衣裳

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (2024 print) (2024), tale 77 'Alimoty and Aliminty' (told by Julia Gentle, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: Jealous of the beloved niece Alimoty, the aunt contracts Lion to kill the girl in the red frock — and each night the frocks are swapped by the girls themselves, so Lion kills the aunt's own daughter, twice, until there are none. Sent to Lion's yard to be killed, Alimoty passes her dead mother's grave, drops the bottle of milk left there, and sings her fate — until the hunter Aliminty hears the voice, comes to the Lion's yard, and kills the Lion.
summary.zh: 嬸母妒忌人人喜愛的姪女阿莉莫蒂，約獅子誅殺穿紅裙者——女孩們夜夜自己調換衣裳，獅子兩次殺的都是嬸母的親生女兒，直至無女可殺。被送赴獅穴途中，阿莉莫蒂經過亡母墳前，失手跌落墓前留下的奶瓶，唱起自己的命運——獵人阿莉明蒂聞聲辨人，趕到獅穴誅獅。

sensitivity.note: Killed-through-swap tale (cruel stepmother type). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: One day a lady had two daughters, but her sister had one; the sister's daughter was named Alimoty, and everybody loved Alimoty but nobody loved the lady's daughters. She went to the Lion and told him he must kill Alimoty for her. The Lion said she must put a red frock on Alimoty and a blue frock on her own daughter when they went to bed. After going to bed, the girl said, 'Cousin Alimoty, your red frock doesn't fit you; let us swap!' — and they swapped, and the Lion killed the lady's daughter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 77 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the lady told the Lion to kill Alimoty, whom everybody loved. 'Tonight you must sew the red frock on Alimoty and the blue frock on your daughter, and I come and kill her tonight.' When they went to bed they swapped again, and the Lion killed the lady's daughter — she had none now. The Lion said, 'Tomorrow send Alimoty to my yard; I will kill her.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 77, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Alimoty was going from the yard and her dead mother gave her a bottle of milk, which she dropped, and she ran off singing — 'Poor me, Alimoty, poor Alimoty, a me Dickie sahnie o-o, see me go long a wid two.' Aliminty was a hunter and heard the singing: 'That is Alimoty's voice!' He came to the Lion's yard and killed the Lion.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 77, ending (1924); not verbatim.
